title: AI Is Rewriting Security’s Job: Your Org Chart Hasn’t Caught Up
summary: As security takes on responsibility for assuring automated systems, its teams need to do more than establish requirements. Our report describes how the cybersecurity function evolves to fulfill that mandate through the trust and assurance organization
body_markdown:
AI is forcing CISOs to reconsider what their organizations are designed to do. Security teams must protect systems, data, and assets while also demonstrating that AI-driven systems operate within approved boundaries. Fulfilling those responsibilities requires CISOs to rethink their teams’ roles, skills, and relationships with the rest of the business. Our latest research[Introducing The Trust And Assurance Organization](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/ai-is-rewriting-securitys-job-your-org-chart-hasnt-caught-up/That%20is%20the%20focus%20of%20Introducing%20The%20Trust%20And%20Assurance%20Organization,%20our%20new%20report%20from%20Madelein%20van%20der%20Hout%20and%20me.%20We%20examine%20how%20the%20cybersecurity%20function%20needs%20to%20evolve%20and%20provide%20a%20starting%20point%20for%20CISOs%20planning%20that%20transition.) (Forrester clients only), examines how the cybersecurity function needs to evolve and provides a starting point for CISOs planning that transition.


### **AI Is Breaking Security’s Old Operating Model**


Agentic AI is becoming part of enterprise operations, even as privacy, security, and governance concerns complicate adoption. Meeting those concerns requires more than new tools or policies and requires security leaders to challenge assumptions about how security work is organized, assigned, and evaluated and address changes head-on, including the reality that:


- **The business is deploying agents faster than it can govern them.** In Forrester’s State Of AI Survey, 2026, 37% of C-level AI decision-makers at enterprises said that six or more of their AI and agentic projects failed before reaching production, and they cited data privacy and security concerns, governance and risk, and trust in agentic systems among the greatest barriers to adoption. Yet boards and executives continue pursuing agents because the economic incentives favor automation, productivity, and scale. This rate of adoption, and the need for trust, expands what security has to do: CISOs must produce defensible evidence that agents, data, models, and automated decisions stay within policy, even when the business units deploying them sit outside security’s control.
- **Security’s own work is also being automated at an unprecedented pace.** As agents take on detection, triage, and response tasks, security teams must determine what those systems can do, when people need to intervene, and how to validate the results. Richard Watson, global cybersecurity consulting leader at EY, told us that for CISO organizations, “the onus is on them to assure that the work is automated rather than doing it themselves.” That shift changes the skills, responsibilities, and structure the security function needs.


### **Evolve Your Remit To Produce Assurance And Earn Trust**


Business leaders still own business decisions and accept the remaining risk, while CISOs remain responsible for demonstrating that security controls work. AI broadens the scope of that responsibility to include automated systems used across the business and within security itself. Security teams must establish requirements, enforce them through technical controls, validate the results, and produce evidence stakeholders can examine. Doing that work requires the authority, skills, and organizational structure to support it.


Enter the trust and assurance organization, or TAO, which Forrester defines as:


*The CISO-led evolution of the cybersecurity function for an era in which digital and AI-driven systems make, recommend, and automate business decisions to protect systems, data, and assets while demonstrating that they operate securely, responsibly, and as intended across the value chain. It uses verifiable controls, governance, evidence, and transparent reporting to attest to the integrity, security, privacy, and responsible use of data and AI and enables stakeholders to determine whether the organization is meeting its obligations.*


The difference between trust and assurance matters. Assurance is the mechanism, which is what the security organization produces: technically enforced controls, continuous validation, and evidence stakeholders can examine. And trust is the outcome, which is what stakeholders decide after they examine that evidence, and it is why security can earn trust but can never certify it.


### **Test Your Security Organization For Authority And Capability Gaps**


To see where you and your current organization stand in terms of TAO capabilities, trace one production AI use case and ask three questions: Who owns the business outcome and accepts the residual risk? Who has the authority to change the agent’s permissions and operating boundaries? What current evidence shows that those boundaries hold? Apply the same logic to one of your automated security workflows. The answers will expose one or both of two gaps:


- **An authority gap.** This is where security is expected to explain an outcome but has no say over the decisions and controls that produced it. Because that gap is a matter of decision rights, to close it, you need to have a discussion with your executive peers about risk and control ownership, as well as reporting lines.
- **A capability gap.** In this gap, security has the right authority but cannot produce the evidence because its functions still depend on periodic reviews and manual handoffs. To close this gap, you must urgently change how the security organization itself is structured, staffed, and measured.


### **Build The TAO Before Someone Else Builds It For You**


Enterprises are already redistributing responsibility for AI governance, identity, data protection, and customer trust, and roles left undefined get assigned through momentum rather than design. You can’t afford to wait for your responsibility to be handed out to you. Use our research, which provides you with a reference organizational chart, explains how eight security functions change, sets out the skills and career paths your teams will need, and replaces activity counts with metrics that show whether controls work.
